chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Unlisted Market — What It Is and How It Works

lessons.title: Grey Market vs the Formal Unlisted Market: What Actually Separates Them

children.text: Meena has moved past WhatsApp brokers entirely. She is now looking at a dealer platform with a clean website, a live "inventory" of unlisted shares across several well-known companies, and a support team that answers her questions within minutes. It feels different from a stranger's WhatsApp forward. Her question is simple: is it actually different, in the ways that matter, or does it just look different?

body.text: "Formal" versus "grey market" for unlisted shares is not about which website looks nicer. It is about whether the shares are ever actually, legally transferred into your name, on a paper trail you can verify independently.

children.text: Two Different Things Called "Grey Market"

markDefs.definition: An unofficial, informally quoted premium on an IPO application or its expected listing price, traded in cash in the days before a specific IPO. It has no legal enforceability and disappears once the stock lists. Unrelated to the ongoing market for an unlisted company's actual shares.

children.text: The phrase "grey market" gets used for two genuinely different things in Indian investing, and mixing them up causes real confusion. Around a specific, already-announced IPO, traders informally quote an
IPO Grey Market Premium (GMP)

, an unofficial premium on where an IPO application or its expected listing price will trade, settled in cash between traders with no legal enforceability. That market exists only in the days and weeks before a specific IPO, and it disappears the moment the stock actually lists. This lesson is about something else entirely: the ongoing, informal buying and selling of an unlisted company's actual shares, months or years before any IPO is even announced, and sometimes when none is ever announced at all.

body.title: Two Unrelated Markets That Share a Name

columns.label: IPO Grey Market Premium (GMP)
points: An unofficial premium on an IPO application or expected listing price, quoted days before that IPO
Exists only around a specific, already-announced IPO
Settled informally, usually in cash, with no legal enforceability
Disappears the moment the stock actually lists

columns.label: Grey Market for Unlisted Shares
points: Informal buying and selling of an unlisted company's actual shares
Can persist for years, for companies with no IPO announced at all
Involves real shares, or claims to real shares, that must eventually be legally transferred

body.text: If someone mentions "grey market" while discussing an unlisted company's shares months before any IPO news, they mean the second kind, the informal market for the shares themselves, not an IPO's GMP. Keep the two separate in your head, because the risks involved are quite different.

children.text: What Actually Makes a Transfer "Formal"

markDefs.definition: The signed contract recording the actual terms of a share sale between a specific named buyer and seller.
The statutory share transfer deed under the Companies Act, 2013, that must be executed and stamped to legally transfer shares of an Indian company.
A company's official record of who owns its shares. A transfer is not complete in law until this register is updated.

children.text: Whatever platform, dealer or WhatsApp contact is involved, transferring shares of an Indian company, listed or not, legally requires the same handful of steps. Buyer and seller sign a
Share Purchase Agreement (SPA)

naming both parties and the exact price and quantity. If the company's Articles include a Right of First Refusal, existing shareholders or the company get a chance to buy first. The company's board approves the transfer, and both parties execute
Form SH-4
, the statutory share transfer deed, with the applicable stamp duty paid. Only once all of this happens does the company update its
Register of Members

, and, for shares held electronically, does the buyer actually see a credit in their own demat account. What makes a transfer "formal" is not the seller's reputation. It is whether these specific steps actually happened.

body.title: What a Legitimate Unlisted Share Transfer Actually Looks Like

events.title: Share Purchase Agreement Signed
events.description: Buyer and seller agree price, quantity and terms in a written, signed agreement naming both parties.

events.title: Right of First Refusal Cleared
events.description: The company or its existing shareholders either waive or do not exercise their Right of First Refusal within the window set by the Articles.

events.title: Board Approval and Form SH-4
events.description: The company's board approves the transfer, and both parties execute Form SH-4, the statutory share transfer deed, with applicable stamp duty paid.

events.title: Payment Through Banking Channels
events.description: The buyer pays via NEFT, RTGS or cheque from their own bank account, directly to the seller, not in cash to an intermediary.

events.title: Demat Credit and Register Update
events.description: Shares are credited to the buyer's demat account via NSDL or CDSL, and the company updates its Register of Members to reflect the new owner.

children.text: What the Grey Market Skips

markDefs.definition: A document authorising one person to act on another's behalf. In the unlisted-share grey market, buyers sometimes receive only a PoA rather than an actual share transfer, meaning the seller keeps legal ownership.

children.text: Informal deals in the unlisted-share grey market routinely skip one or more of these steps. Payment sometimes goes in cash, or into a middleman's personal bank account rather than the actual seller's. Documentation is often a one-page note or a WhatsApp message rather than a signed SPA. And in a meaningful share of cases, the buyer never actually receives the shares at all. Instead, they receive a
Power of Attorney (PoA)
, a document letting them act on the seller's behalf, while the seller quietly keeps legal title to the shares.

body.text: A Power of Attorney is not ownership. The seller remains the shares' legal owner and can, in principle, sell the same block to someone else, refuse to cooperate later, or simply become unreachable. If a dispute arises, a PoA holder has a far weaker legal position than someone whose name is actually on the company's Register of Members.

body.caption: Formal transfer vs grey market deal, side by side

cells: Traceable, via banking channels, into the seller's own account
Often cash, or paid into an unrelated middleman's personal account
Signed SPA, executed Form SH-4, board resolution copies
A verbal promise or a one-page WhatsApp-shared note
Shares actually credited to the buyer's demat account; Register of Members updated
Often just a Power of Attorney; legal title may never actually move
Buyer can independently confirm the holding via demat statement and company or RTA records
Buyer has no independent way to confirm they own anything

body.label: The single test that matters
body.value: Is it actually in your demat account?
body.context: If an unlisted share purchase never results in a credit to your own CDSL or NSDL demat account, you do not legally own it, whatever documents a dealer has shown you.

children.text: How to Actually Check Before You Pay

body.title: Before Paying for Any Unlisted Share Deal
steps: Insist on a written Share Purchase Agreement naming the actual seller, not just a dealer or intermediary
Pay only via a traceable banking channel (NEFT, RTGS or cheque), directly to the seller's own bank account, never to a personal account described as an "escrow"
Confirm the company has actually approved the transfer and that Form SH-4 has been executed with stamp duty paid
After the deal, check your own CDSL or NSDL demat statement to confirm the shares were actually credited, not just told that they were
Avoid any deal where the "ownership" offered is only a Power of Attorney rather than an actual share transfer

children.text: Are Dealer Platforms Any Safer Than a WhatsApp Broker?

Dealer platforms that specialise in unlisted shares, names like UnlistedZone, Precize and Stockify come up often, are generally more accountable than an anonymous WhatsApp number. They have a business identity, an operating history, and real reputational risk if they cheat customers. None of that makes them a SEBI-regulated stock exchange, and none of it substitutes for the verification steps above. A polished website is a better sales interface. It is not, by itself, proof that a transfer will be properly documented.

body.text: Treat a professional-looking platform and a WhatsApp broker the same way procedurally: verify the SPA, verify the payment destination, verify Form SH-4, and verify the demat credit yourself. The only real difference a good platform should make is that it has less reason to skip these steps in the first place, not that you get to skip checking them.

body.title: Pay First, Transfer Later?
body.scenario: The dealer platform Meena is now looking at has a clean website, lists "available inventory" of shares in several well-known unlisted companies, and asks for payment upfront into the platform's own current account before it will "process the transfer", promising demat credit "within 30 to 45 working days".
body.prompt: Is this materially different from the WhatsApp broker's offer, and what should Meena insist on before paying?
body.modelAnswer: Paying into the platform's own account rather than the actual seller's account, on a vague 30-to-45-day promise, with no signed SPA naming the real seller shown upfront, still leaves Meena without a documented, traceable transfer at the point she pays. She should insist on seeing a signed SPA naming the actual seller before any money moves, ask explicitly whether her payment goes directly to the seller or is held by the platform (and if held, what protects her if the transfer fails), get a written commitment with a specific date for demat credit, and independently check her own demat account herself once that window passes rather than relying on the platform's word. A polished interface may reduce some execution risk compared with an anonymous broker, but it does not remove the need for these checks.

body.title: What Actually Proves Ownership
body.question: What is the single most reliable proof that an unlisted share transfer to you was actually completed?
options: A signed agreement from the dealer confirming the sale
A WhatsApp message from the seller confirming payment received
The shares appearing as a credit in your own CDSL or NSDL demat account statement
An invoice or receipt issued by the dealer platform
body.explanation: Only an actual credit to your own demat account, verifiable independently through your depository participant, confirms legal ownership. Agreements, messages and invoices can all exist without a transfer ever actually being completed.

body.title: What You Get Instead of Ownership
body.textWithBlank: In the informal unlisted-share market, shares are sometimes not actually transferred to the buyer at all; instead the buyer receives only a ___, while the seller keeps legal title to the shares.
body.explanation: A Power of Attorney only authorises the holder to act on the seller's behalf. It does not, by itself, transfer legal ownership of the shares.

body.title: Grey Market vs Formal Transfer: Key Terms

cards.definition: An unofficial, informally quoted premium on an IPO application or expected listing price in the days before a specific IPO. Unrelated to the ongoing grey market for unlisted company shares.
The signed contract recording the actual terms of a share sale between a specific named buyer and seller.
The statutory share transfer deed under the Companies Act, 2013, that must be executed and stamped to legally transfer shares of an Indian company.
An informal structure where a buyer holds only a document authorising them to act on the seller's behalf, while legal ownership of the shares never actually transfers.
The institutions that hold dematerialised shares electronically. A credit to your demat account through one of these is the definitive proof of ownership.
A company's official record of who owns its shares. A transfer is not complete in law until this register is updated.

points: "Grey market" for unlisted shares is different from the IPO "grey market premium (GMP)" you may have heard about around a specific IPO. Do not confuse the two.

A legally complete share transfer requires a signed agreement, company or board approval, an executed Form SH-4, and an actual credit to the buyer's demat account, whatever platform or broker is involved.
The grey market for unlisted shares often skips one or more of these steps, most dangerously the actual demat credit, leaving buyers holding only a Power of Attorney and no real legal title.
A professional-looking dealer platform is not automatically a safer transaction. It is a better sales interface. The underlying legal steps still need to be verified.
The single most reliable proof of ownership is an actual credit visible in your own CDSL or NSDL demat account statement, checked independently rather than taken on a seller's or dealer's word.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Meena is fictional and used purely for illustration. Names of dealer platforms mentioned are used only as examples of the category and are not endorsements or warnings about any specific platform. Always independently verify a seller's identity, the transfer documentation, and your own demat credit before paying for any unlisted share.
